say: You give it an equation with $x$ on one or both sides. It finds the one value of $\hl{2}{x}$ that makes both sides equal.
The key idea: whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Use that to get every $x$ term on one side and every number on the other.

how.higher: Higher level almost never asks for it alone. It is the last step inside a bigger part: finding an unknown in a line, a sequence or a function, on both papers.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it directly, usually as part (a) of an early Paper 1 question, worth 5 to 15 marks. It is a main skill in 12 parts over 11 years.

steps.title: Remove the bracket
steps.say: Multiply every term in the bracket by $4$. Then tidy the numbers on the left.

steps.title: Collect the x terms
steps.say: Take $\hl{1}{2x}$ from both sides so the $x$ terms are on the left. Then add $7$ to both sides so the numbers are on the right.

lines.text: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

steps.title: Divide to find x
steps.say: Divide both sides by $2$ to leave $\hl{2}{x}$ on its own.

steps.title: Check the answer
steps.say: Put $x = 8$ back into the original equation. Both sides must match.

higher.tip: If the question does not say how to solve it, still solve it by algebra. Checking a guess in the equation is only accepted as supporting work, not as the method.

sources.quote: If equation is not solved algebraically

higher.tip: Writing the equation down correctly earns marks before you solve it. Show that setup line.

sources.quote: Work of merit in establishing equation

ordinary.tip: The marks follow the steps: remove the bracket, move terms across, then solve. Show each one.
Multiply every term in the bracket. Missing one loses the first step.
Transposing (moving terms across the equals sign) is its own step in the scheme. Do it on a separate line.
Even one correct operation earns something, so never leave the part blank.

say: You give it a linear equation where the $x$ terms sit over numbers, like $\frac{x+3}{2}$. It finds $\hl{2}{x}$ the same way as any linear equation, once the fractions are gone.
The key idea: multiply **every** term by the common denominator. The fractions cancel and a plain linear equation is left.

how.higher: Higher level never tests it as a part of its own. It appears inside bigger parts, such as a mean with an unknown frequency or a speed and time problem.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it directly as part (a) of an early Paper 1 question, worth 10 marks. It is a main skill in 3 parts over 11 years.

steps.title: Find the common denominator
steps.say: The denominators are $2$ and $4$. The smallest number both go into is $\hl{1}{4}$.

steps.title: Multiply every term
steps.say: Multiply each term by $\hl{1}{4}$, including the $5$ on the right. Each fraction cancels.

lines.text: The $5$ on the right is multiplied too. It is easy to forget.

steps.title: Tidy the left side
steps.say: Remove the bracket and collect the $x$ terms and the numbers.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Take $5$ from both sides, then divide by $3$.

ordinary.tip: Name the common denominator. The scheme gives marks for identifying it.
Some correct multiplication is worth marks even if the rest goes wrong. Show it line by line.
You may find the answer by trial and improvement, but only if you verify the value for full marks.

say: You give it an equation with $x$ under a square root, like $\sqrt{f(x)} = g(x)$. It finds the values of $x$ that really work.
The key idea: square both sides to remove the root. Squaring can add false answers, so every solution must be **checked** in the original equation.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it as a 10 mark part of its own on Paper 1 (2024) and as a step inside longer applied parts, such as a time or distance problem. It is a main skill in 5 parts over 11 years.

steps.title: Square both sides
steps.say: Square both sides to remove the root. Square the whole of $x + 2$, not each term.

steps.title: Make a quadratic
steps.say: Move everything to one side so it equals $0$, then factorise.

steps.title: Test x = 2
steps.say: Put $x = 2$ into the original equation, not the squared one.

lines.text: The sides are $1$ and $-1$. They are not equal, so reject $x = -3$.

higher.tip: If a wrong root is left in, you lose a mark. Check each solution in the original equation and cross out the one that fails.

sources.quote: Apply a * for incorrect solution(s) not

higher.tip: Getting the squared quadratic right is worth its own credit. Write that line clearly.

sources.quote: Fully correct quadratic (2nd line in solution)

higher.tip: Write out a check of each solution. The marking notes show it as part of the model answer.
When more than one root comes out, say which one you are keeping.

say: You give it an equation where $x$ sits in the denominators, like $\frac{1}{x}$. It finds the values of $\hl{2}{x}$ that solve it.
The key idea: multiply every term by the common denominator to clear the fractions. That leaves a quadratic. Then check that no answer makes a denominator $0$.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it rarely: once on Paper 1 (2019) as a 15 mark part, where clearing the fractions gives a quadratic.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it rarely too: once on Paper 1 (2018), as a 15 mark part where clearing the fractions gives a quadratic.

steps.title: Common denominator
steps.say: The denominators are $x$, $x + 2$ and $4$. Their common denominator is $\hl{1}{4x(x + 2)}$. $x$ cannot be $0$ or $-2$.

steps.title: Clear the fractions
steps.say: Multiply every term by $\hl{1}{4x(x + 2)}$. Each fraction cancels.

steps.title: Make a quadratic
steps.say: Move everything to the right side so one side is $0$. Then factorise.

steps.title: Read off the roots
steps.say: Each bracket can be $0$. Check neither answer is $0$ or $-2$.

lines.text: Neither is $0$ or $-2$, so both are allowed.

higher.tip: Reach an equation with no fractions first. That is a marked stage on its own.
Name the common denominator. Even identifying it earns marks.

ordinary.tip: Name the common denominator. It is marked on its own.
